rows.anchor: Closed-world assumption: If it isn't recorded, assume false. ... Open-world assumption: If it isn't recorded, truth status remains unknown. For epistemic engineering, many knowledge questions require the second. This is particularly important for AI agents. ... Unknown ≠ False.
rows.statement: KnowledgeOS should explicitly distinguish closed-world assumption ('if it isn't recorded, assume false') from open-world assumption ('if it isn't recorded, truth status remains unknown'), arguing epistemic-engineering questions -- especially for AI agents -- generally require the open-world reading; restates the invariant Unknown != False and warns 'no evidence found' must not be conflated with 'evidence does not exist.'

rows.anchor: Unknown must be a legitimate state. Not: Unknown = False. Not: Unknown = Null either. Because null is a technical representation, while UNKNOWN is semantic. ... L = {True,False,Unknown}. For some verification operations we may need: {Pass,Fail,Inconclusive}. These are related but not identical. Verification = INCONCLUSIVE does not necessarily imply Claim = UNKNOWN.
rows.statement: Unknown must be a legitimate semantic state, distinct from both False (Unknown!=False) and from a technical Null (Unknown!=Null, since null is a technical representation while UNKNOWN is semantic). Proposes a three-valued epistemic logic L={True,False,Unknown} alongside a related but non-identical verification-outcome logic {Pass,Fail,Inconclusive}; a Verification=INCONCLUSIVE result does not necessarily imply Claim=UNKNOWN since the verification method itself may simply lack sufficient evidence. Restates the statistical-discipline rule: 'no evidence' implies 'insufficient evidence', not 'negative conclusion', unless a closed-world rule is explicitly declared for the domain.

notations: e,w |= O alpha iff forall w': w' in e iff e,w'|=alpha

sources.note: Formal O operator: e |= O alpha iff e consists exactly of the worlds where alpha is true, i.e. 'alpha is ALL that is known'; characterizes ASK/TELL via |=(OKB=>Kalpha) and |=(OKB=>K(alpha==phi)); a 'determinate' sentence uniquely determines an epistemic state and every determinate sentence is equivalent (under O) to some objective sentence -- proposed as the formal basis for KnowledgeOS Zero ('having a KB means these sentences are all that is known... implies not believing others').

rows.anchor: e,w\models O\alpha \iff for every w', w'\in e \iff e,w'\models\alpha ... alpha is all that is known ... ASK[\alpha,\Re[KB]]=YES\iff\models(OKB\supset K\alpha) ... A sentence delta is determinate if it uniquely determines an epistemic state ... for any determinate sentence delta, there is an objective sentence phi such that \models O\delta\equiv O\phi
rows.statement: Full formal Only-Knowing O operator (e consists exactly of the alpha-worlds), its ASK/TELL characterizations via O, and the determinate-sentence theorem (every determinate sentence is O-equivalent to some objective sentence) -- the formal basis for the Representation Theorem and the strongest available candidate formalization of 'all that is known' for the Zero TODO.

rows.anchor: Having a knowledge base means that these sentences are all that is known. ... having an incomplete knowledge base means knowing where that knowledge is incomplete. ... Armed with this meta-knowledge, an agent is in a position to do something better than giving up ... it can apply a default, perform sensing, ask a question ... enables the agent to know what it does not know.
rows.statement: Four key quotes arguing Zero should mean KNOWING that nothing is missing (not merely having no known gaps), that incompleteness itself should be meta-known so the agent can act on it (apply a default, sense, ask), and that the main justification for an agent reasoning about its own knowledge is enabling it to know what it does not know -- directly relevant to, and possibly in tension with, this batch's other 'Zero cannot be known as Zero' argument (Fitch's-paradox translation in S2530) and the structural-unknowability classification (S2528).

sources.note: S0705: Stewart Shapiro's 'Thinking About Mathematics: The Philosophy of Mathematics' (Oxford, 2000), a 321-page scanned-image PDF with no extractable text layer, present in the brainstorming corpus as an uploaded reference work. Structured in four parts: I Perspective (ch1-2, overview of the field and its central questions), II History (ch3 Plato & Aristotle, ch4 Kant & Mill), III The Big Three (ch5 Logicism, ch6 Formalism, ch7 Intuitionism), IV The Contemporary Scene (ch8 realism/Platonism about mathematical objects, ch9 anti-realist/nominalist views, ch10 Structuralism -- the author's own position). No companion KnowledgeOS extraction document for this book exists in this batch.

rows.anchor: PART I. PERSPECTIVE ... PART II. HISTORY ... PART III. THE BIG THREE ... PART IV. THE CONTEMPORARY SCENE ... 10 STRUCTURALISM 1. The Underlying Idea 2. Ante Rem Structures, and Objects 3. Structuralism Without Structures 4. Knowledge of Structures ... This is my own position (Shapiro 1997), so one might say that I have saved the best for last.
rows.statement: The book is organized into four parts: Part I Perspective (ch.1 what is interesting about mathematics for a philosopher; ch.2 a potpourri of central questions -- necessity/a priori knowledge, objects/objectivity/truth, the mathematical vs the physical, theorems/theories/concepts); Part II History (ch.3 Plato and Aristotle; ch.4 Kant and Mill); Part III The Big Three (ch.5 Logicism -- Frege, Russell, Carnap/logical positivism; ch.6 Formalism -- Hilbert's Grundlagen der Geometrie, finitism, incompleteness, Curry; ch.7 Intuitionism -- Brouwer, Heyting, Dummett); Part IV The Contemporary Scene (ch.8 realism about mathematical objects -- Godel, web of belief, set-theoretic realism; ch.9 anti-realism -- fictionalism, modal construction; ch.10 Structuralism -- ante rem structures, structuralism without structures, knowledge of structures via pattern recognition and implicit definition), explicitly identified by the author as his own position ('I have saved the best for last').

rows.path: docs/knowledgeos/brainstorming/Thinking about mathematics - The philosophy of mathematics (2000) (Stewart Shapiro) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
rows.anchor: Rationalism is a long-standing philosophical school that can be characterized as an attempt to extend the perceived methodology of mathematics to all of knowledge. ... The main opposition to rationalism is empiricism, the view that sense experience, and not pure reason, is the source of knowledge. ... mathematical knowledge seems to be based on proof, not observation, mathematics is an apparent counterexample to the main empiricist thesis. Indeed, mathematics is sometimes held up as a paradigm of a priori knowledge.
rows.statement: Frames Chapter 1's opening problem: rationalism attempts to extend mathematics' perceived methodology (proof, pure reason) to all of knowledge (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz), while empiricism holds sense experience, not pure reason, is the source of knowledge (Locke, Berkeley, Hume, Mill, later logical positivists); mathematics is an apparent counterexample to empiricism since mathematical knowledge seems based on proof rather than observation, making it a paradigm case of a priori knowledge (knowledge prior to and independent of experience) that empiricists have historically struggled to accommodate.

rows.path: docs/knowledgeos/brainstorming/Thinking about mathematics - The philosophy of mathematics (2000) (Stewart Shapiro) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
rows.anchor: There are several reasons for the connection between mathematics and philosophy. Both are among the first intellectual attempts to understand the world around us ... mathematics is an important case study for the philosopher. Many issues on the agenda of contemporary philosophy have remarkably clean formulations when focused on mathematics. ... A third reason ... lies in epistemology ... mathematics is a primary tool in our best efforts to understand the world. ... Galileo wrote that the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics. This insightful, enigmatic metaphor highlights the place of mathematics in the scientific/philosophical enterprise of understanding the world, but it does not even hint at a solution of the problem.
rows.statement: Gives three reasons for the mathematics-philosophy connection: (1) both fields share ancient shared origins and undergo definitional transformations over what counts as each discipline; (2) mathematics is a clean case study for general philosophical questions of reference (what does a term stand for/represent?) and normativity (what obligates correct reasoning?), since mathematics and logic provide simple, well-formulated cases; (3) mathematics is epistemologically central because it is a primary tool for scientific understanding of the physical, human, and social world -- quoting Galileo's 'the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics' as an insightful but unsolved metaphor for why mathematics plays this role.
missing: why mathematics specifically enables understanding of the physical/social world

rows.path: docs/knowledgeos/brainstorming/Thinking about mathematics - The philosophy of mathematics (2000) (Stewart Shapiro) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
rows.anchor: To what extent can we expect philosophy to determine or even suggest the proper practice of mathematics? Conversely, to what extent can we expect the autonomous practice of mathematics to determine the correct philosophy of mathematics? ... Plato ... held that the subject-matter of mathematics is an eternal, unchanging, ideal realm. ... he complained that mathematicians do not know what they are talking about ... [They] speak as if they were doing something and as if all their words were directed toward action ... whereas in fact the real object of the entire subject is ... knowledge ... of what eternally exists ... Virtually every source of ancient geometry, including Euclid's Elements, makes extensive use of constructive, dynamic language ... If Plato's philosophy is correct, dynamic language makes no sense.
rows.statement: Chapter 2 poses the 'chicken or egg' question: to what extent should philosophy determine/suggest proper mathematical practice, versus to what extent should autonomous mathematical practice determine the correct philosophy of mathematics. Illustrated via Plato (Republic Book 7): mathematics' subject matter is an eternal, unchanging, ideal realm, so geometers who speak in active/constructive language ('draw a line', 'construct a figure') are speaking incorrectly, since the real object of study is timeless knowledge, not action -- yet virtually all ancient geometry (including Euclid's Elements) uses exactly this constructive, dynamic language, producing the tension: if Plato's philosophy is correct, dynamic mathematical language makes no sense, generating a genuine counterexample/tension between the philosophical view and actual mathematical practice.

rationale_evidence.statement: Gives three reasons for the mathematics-philosophy connection: (1) both fields share ancient shared origins and undergo definitional transformations over what counts as each discipline; (2) mathematics is a clean case study for general philosophical questions of reference (what does a term stand for/represent?) and normativity (what obligates correct reasoning?), since mathematics and logic provide simple, well-formulated cases; (3) mathematics is epistemologically central because it is a primary tool for scientific understanding of the physical, human, and social world -- quoting Galileo's 'the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics' as an insightful but unsolved metaphor for why mathematics plays this role.

rows.statement: Claim Maturity Ladder: OBSERVED ('X occurred') -> DESCRIPTIVE ('X occurred more frequently in group A') -> ASSOCIATIVE ('X is associated with Y') -> EXPLANATORY ('Mechanism M may explain the relationship') -> CAUSAL ('X causes Y'), each level requiring progressively more evidence and identification; governance can then bind ClaimType=CAUSAL to required artifacts (ResearchDesign, AssumptionLedger, RivalExplanationAnalysis, IdentificationAssessment, EvidenceConvergence, Validation) versus lighter requirements for ClaimType=DESCRIPTIVE, described as 'policy-driven epistemic governance.'

sources.note: Step 180 proposes a first-class Investigation object <Question,Scope,Hypothesis,RequiredEvidence,Owner,Status,Outcome> giving the pipeline Unknown->Investigation->Evidence->Determination, a mechanism moving from uncertainty toward knowledge. rows.statement: Grounds the biological-metaphor protocol in two concrete, non-biological distributed-systems test cases: Test Case 1 maps an HTTP request/timeout scenario (client sends a request, service times out) against a matched non-communicative control (local disk read-speed degradation), showing the diagnostic inquiry 'why did the service fail?' remains unresolved while the actionable inquiry 'should the client fail over?' is decisively resolved by policy -- demonstrating Actionable Closure != Epistemic Closure concretely; Test Case 2 maps a database lock-request/deny-challenge/force-release/grant sequence, showing that an intermediate challenge-and-response cycle can potentially be removed (Zero) if a later action alone achieves the same final lock state, giving a concrete emergent-Zero testing ground.

experiment.hypothesis: The Actionable-Closure/Epistemic-Closure and item-vs-sequence Zero distinctions proposed via the biological metaphor are demonstrable in ordinary distributed-software communication logs, not only in biological signalling.
experiment.setup: Two concrete scenarios: an HTTP client/service timeout with a non-networked control, and a database lock request/challenge/release sequence.
experiment.assumptions: Distributed-systems communication logs are a valid proxy domain for testing the same structural distinctions the biological lens proposed.
experiment.inputs: HTTP request/timeout logs; database lock-sequence logs.
experiment.method: Apply the KR-BIOCOMM-ZERO-01 measurement scheme (Zero_Q, Determination, Decision) to each logged sequence.
experiment.result: Not yet executed in this document -- presented as illustrative worked test-case designs.
experiment.interpretation: If concrete software systems reproduce the same closure/Zero distinctions, this would validate the protocol's applicability beyond biology.
experiment.limitations: These are illustrative designs, not executed experimental results.
experiment.conclusion: Provides a concrete, implementable path for testing the biologically-motivated Zero-space hypotheses without relying on animal-behavior claims.
